claims.text: Enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance in MPEAs is governed by rapid formation of a multicomponent oxide scale.
The multicomponent oxide scale preserves material integrity during high-temperature exposure.
The protective oxide scale is self-healing.
Oxide-scale evolution is mediated by coupled, rate-limiting diffusion of Cr, Al, and Mn.
An optimal balance of Cr, Al, and Mn produces faster protective-scale formation than reducing one or more of those elements.
The relevant protective structure can be a layered MnCr2O4/Al2O3 scale.
A protective structure can instead contain an outer MnCr2O4 layer and an inner Cr2O3 layer.
The layered oxide scale acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
Defect engineering can create fast diffusion paths that accelerate delivery of protective-scale-forming elements.
Optimizing Cr, Al, and Mn concentrations enhances their coupled diffusion.
Enhanced coupled diffusion accelerates formation of a coherent oxide scale.
Optimizing Cr, Al, and Mn causes oxidation kinetics to transition from a diffusion-limited parabolic regime to a more stable steady-state regime.
The optimized MPEA will form a multilayer oxide scale more rapidly than the baseline alloy.
The optimized MPEA will have a lower parabolic oxidation rate constant than the baseline alloy.
The optimized MPEA will retain better mechanical integrity than the baseline after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
An alloy with lower concentrations of one or more of Cr, Al, and Mn will exhibit conventional parabolic oxidation and poorer structural integrity.
The proposed mechanism applies above 500 °C and particularly from 900 °C to 1100 °C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at lower temperatures or where degradation mechanisms other than oxidation dominate.

contradictions.description: Diffusion is described as rate-limiting and governing scale evolution, yet the proposed optimization is also said to move oxidation away from a diffusion-limited regime. The relevant diffusion stages and rate-controlling step are not distinguished.

The hypothesis predicts a transition away from parabolic kinetics while also using a reduced parabolic rate constant as an expected outcome. It does not specify whether the parabolic constant applies before the transition or how a near-steady-state regime will be distinguished.
